newsitem.title: CANADA: Markets relieved as Canada Liberals re-elected.
newsitem.headline: Markets relieved as Canada Liberals re-elected.

text.p: Canadian financial markets breathed a sigh of relief on Tuesday after the ruling Liberal Party won a slim majority in Canada's parliament.
The Canadian dollar slid almost one Canadian cent late on Monday as early results from the Atlantic provinces showed heavy losses for the Liberals.
"With the initial Atlantic provinces results, we tanked to the C$1.3830 (72.30 U.S. cent) level," said Stephen Wateridge director of corporate foreign exchange at CIBC-Wood Gundy Inc.

But the dollar rallied to Monday's closing levels around C$1.3730 (72.83 U.S. cents) after the Liberals won 101 of 103 seats in vote-rich Ontario, helping them secure a slim majority of 155 seats in Canada's 301-seat parliament.
Canadian bonds had been expected to rally if the Liberals won a convincing majority, but analysts said the narrow win gave the market little cause for celebration.
"Fiscally I don't think there are any changes, but the slight majority might be reining in enthusiasm," said Harv Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A.

Canada's 30-year benchmark bond fell C10 cents (7 cents) to C$112.37 ($81.84) to yield 7.007 percent, while the U.S. 30-year bond traded unchanged to yield 6.90 percent. The spread between the two bonds widened to 11 basis points from 10 basis points at Monday's close.
Toronto stocks opened flat on Tuesday, after equity analysts had time to break down the election results.

Canadians elected the right-wing, Western Canada-based Reform Party as the official opposition with 60 seats, ousting the separatist Bloc Quebecois. But the Bloc won 44 of the 75 seats in the French-speaking province of Quebec, indicating continued separatist strength.
Despite their thin majority, economists reassured investors that the Liberals would easily meet and likely exceed their plans for slashing Canada's budget deficit.

The government said recently that its 1996-97 deficit would probably not exceed C$16 billion ($11.65 billion) -- much lower than its stated target of C$19 billion ($13.83 billion). Economists said they expected the deficit may be even lower.

"They are way ahead of plans," said Craig Wright, assistant chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada. "I guess with them being so far ahead, there is some room to accelerate the expected tax reforms, so maybe we'll see some tinkering."
